ideas.note: Three today: one about road geometry, one about doors propped open by exasperated staff, and one that makes clients multiply.

archive.build: Single page at /security/run-up/. SVG for the editable road (polyline with draggable vertices) and canvas for the vehicle animation and energy bar, all in plain JavaScript. Main work: the path editor, sampling curvature along the path to set the corner speed caps, a 1D kinematics integrator, the comparison overlay and some plain-English captions. Values are kept abstract and relative, with no crash ratings, vehicle masses or site data.
archive.pitch: Draw the road and see the energy. A forecourt sits at the bottom of a black canvas and you sketch the approach in white lines. A generic block vehicle accelerates down it, and an energy bar fills in a single amber accent as it reaches the line. Straight roads light the bar up; a couple of well-placed bends drain it.
archive.title: Run-Up
archive.theory: Hostile vehicle mitigation and vehicle dynamics: impact energy is ½mv², so doubling speed quadruples it. On a straight r
archive.takeaway: You do not just stop a vehicle at the line. You decide how fast it can possibly arrive, and geometry does a lot of that work for free.
archive.how_it_works: The visitor drags out a road corridor from the top of the screen to a protected frontage. They can add up to three corners, or drop in landscaping blocks to narrow and kink the route. A deliberately generic vehicle, with no make, mass class or rating, runs the route on a simple model. It accelerates on straights. On bends it is capped by a friendly cornering limit, shown as a ghost speedometer arc. A live readout shows speed and relative energy as a multiple of a 'walking pace' baseline. When it reaches the frontage, a thin line marks the stand-off and the energy bar freezes. A second run can be overlaid so the visitor can compare layouts. A 'quadruple' toast appears the first time they discover that doubling the speed means four times the energy. The run ends with a one-line verdict ('long straight: energy high, harder problem to stop'), with no pass or fail against real products.

archive.build: Single page at /security/propped-open/. Canvas for the agents and plan, with plain JavaScript for a small agent loop (waypoint routing, queue model, friction accumulator and workaround spawner) and SVG for the dials and end chart. Main work: tuning the control values so there is a clear sweet spot, workaround sprites in line style, and the end-of-week summary copy.
archive.pitch: You run an office for a simulated week. Add controls and watch your little white staff dots get slower, crosser and more creative. Push too hard and doors start glowing red as they are wedged open behind your back.
archive.title: Propped Open
archive.theory: The security–convenience trade-off and usable security: every control adds friction, and past a point people work around
archive.takeaway: Security that people route around is theatre. The best control is often the one nobody notices using.
archive.how_it_works: A top-down line plan shows an entrance, lifts, a kitchen and a server room, with around 40 staff dots moving between them. A toolbar offers controls: turnstiles, a second badge reader, a PIN pad, mandatory escorts, password expiry and a visitor sign-in. Each control has a security value and a friction cost, and friction shows as dots queuing and a mood meter dipping. Once local friction crosses a threshold, workarounds spawn. A door gets propped, rendered in the one accent colour. A badge passes between two dots. A note appears stuck on a monitor. Two dials run along the top: Nominal Security, which only goes up as you add controls, and Actual Security, which subtracts the workarounds. The week plays out at 30 seconds a day, and the visitor can also remove controls or add friction-free options such as better signage, a faster reader or a staffed reception that greets people. Friday ends with a chart of both lines over the week and a rating.

archive.build: Single page at /security/times-table/. SVG grid and draggable cards in plain JavaScript, with simple tween animations for the reveal and sort. Main work: writing ten generic, non-site-specific scenarios with reference placements and short rationales, the treatment-token round, and the twist explainer. There is no backend and nothing is stored.
archive.pitch: Ten generic scenario cards to drop onto a 5×5 grid. Then the grid does maths at you and shows where your gut and the numbers disagree.
archive.title: Times Table
archive.theory: Risk = likelihood × impact, and the limits of the risk matrix. Ordinal 5×5 scores compress very different risks into the
archive.takeaway: Risk is a product, not a feeling. A single score hides which half of the sum you should be working on.
archive.how_it_works: Cards such as 'laptop left on a train', 'flood in the basement plant room', 'tailgater at reception' and 'regional power outage' appear one at a time as white line icons. The visitor drags each one onto a likelihood × impact grid drawn in thin white lines. Once all ten are placed, the reveal animates. Each cell's score fades in, the cards sort themselves into a ranked list, and a ghost card slides to a reference position from an illustrative 'consultant's view'. Distance is shown as a dotted line, with the biggest disagreement in accent colour. In round two the visitor gets three treatment tokens. Each token moves one card either down (likelihood) or left (impact), and they watch the total risk score fall. A final twist card shows two risks sharing a score of 5: one at likelihood 5 × impact 1 and one at likelihood 1 × impact 5. It asks 'are these really the same?' and gives a short explainer on why rare, severe risks need separate judgement. The quiz ends with a 'risk instinct' score that is light on blame.

archive.build: A single page at /security/three-sides/ drawn on canvas in plain JavaScript. The main pieces of work are: a routine scheduler (agents following waypoint lists keyed to the clock); a proximity check per place; drag-and-drop tokens with a radius of influence; an SVG triangle and controllers diagram that animates in sync; and the end-of-day timeline. No data stored.
archive.pitch: A little white-line town runs on clockwork routines. Commuters, shops, bike racks and a few loiterers move along their daily paths. Whenever an offender, a target and an empty place line up, a triangle snaps shut in accent orange. Your job is to stop the triangles closing, and you never touch the offender directly.
archive.title: Three Sides
archive.theory: Routine activity theory and the crime triangle: a crime needs a motivated offender and a suitable target to meet in the
archive.takeaway: Crime is mostly ordinary routines crossing at the wrong time and place. You can prevent it by removing any one side of the triangle, and the cheapest side to remove is often not the offender.
archive.how_it_works: A top-down line map shows a station, high street, park and car park. Dots follow timed routines through a 24-hour day that runs in about 90 seconds. When an offender dot and a target dot sit at the same unguarded place, the three sides of a triangle draw themselves and hold for a beat before a small mark counts it as an incident. You get a limited budget of tokens to drag on: Guardian (a neighbour, a shop assistant, a patrol), Handler (a parent, a youth worker, a probation officer) and Manager (a caretaker, a landlord, a park keeper). Each token greys out one side of the triangle within its reach, and the triangle can only close if all three sides are live. The outer ring of the triangle diagram, Eck's controllers, lights up to show which side you broke. Each round reshuffles the routines, adding a late-night economy or a school run, so a fix that worked at noon fails at 2am. You win a day by keeping incidents under a target. A final replay shows a 24-hour clock coloured by where and when the triangles nearly closed.

archive.build: A single page at /security/morning-rush/ in plain JavaScript. The lobby animation is on canvas and the gauges and end chart are SVG. The main pieces of work are: an arrival generator weighted towards nine o'clock; a queue model per lane; per-gate-type parameters for throughput and follow-through behaviour (illustrative values, labelled as such); the propped-door rule; and the persistent results chart kept in memory only.
archive.pitch: It is 08:45 in a corporate lobby and 400 people want to get in before nine. You pick the gate and watch what happens: a swing door that everyone holds open politely, a waist-high turnstile, glass speed lanes, or a full-height single-person interlock. A tailgater shows up in accent colour whenever a second person slips through on one swipe.
archive.title: Morning Rush
archive.theory: The security-convenience trade-off in access control. Every gate type balances throughput, cost and resistance to tailga
archive.takeaway: No gate is simply 'secure'. Each one is a point on a curve, and pushing too hard on security without enough capacity creates workarounds that are worse than a modest control people actually use.
archive.how_it_works: A side-on line drawing of a lobby, with staff arriving as small walking figures whose arrivals bunch up towards nine o'clock. You choose the gate type, the number of lanes, whether a guard or reception desk watches the line, and a staff 'patience' slider. Each gate has a characteristic throughput and its own chance of letting someone follow through, and those chances rise as the queue grows and people get impatient. Live gauges show average wait, queue length, count of tailgates and an 'annoyance' meter. When the annoyance meter gets high, a fire door at the side may start getting propped open, drawn in red, and it lets anyone in. The run ends at 09:15 with a scatter plot: your configuration appears as a dot on a throughput-versus-tailgating chart, alongside your earlier attempts, so you can trace the trade-off curve yourself.

archive.build: A single page at /security/pinch-point/ with a canvas simulation of a few hundred agents in plain JavaScript using a spatial grid. The main pieces of work are: the agent steering rules; density sampling on a grid for the heat map; an editable wall and exit layer; the SVG fundamental-diagram panel and flow strip; and three preset layouts. Thresholds are presented as indicative, with a plain-English note pointing to the Green Guide and Martyn's Law context.
archive.pitch: A full venue concourse empties in real time as a swarm of white dots. Where the crowd thickens, the floor fills in like a heat map, faint grey for comfortable and rising to accent red where density gets dangerous. You redraw the exits and barriers and see the red bloom shrink, or move somewhere else.
archive.title: Pinch Point
archive.theory: Crowd density and flow in egress. Flow through an exit is limited by its width and by how dense the crowd is. As density
archive.takeaway: Crowds do not jam because of panic. They jam because of geometry. Balanced exits, no sudden narrowing and no merges keep density low, and density is what hurts people.
archive.how_it_works: A plan view of a generic event space (not a real site) with a few exits. Pressing 'Event ends' releases a crowd that steers towards the nearest exit using simple local rules: keep a personal-space radius, avoid walls and slow down as local density rises. A live strip along the bottom plots people out per minute for each exit, next to a running count of 'red seconds', the time any area spends above a high-density threshold. The visitor can widen or narrow exits, add or remove barrier lines, open a second door, add signage that nudges some people towards a less obvious exit, or switch on a counter-flow (people coming back in for a lost friend). Presets show classic lessons: a funnel that narrows, two streams merging at a corner, and one popular exit while another sits empty. The run ends when the venue is clear, and the score is the clearance time plus red seconds. A small explainer shows the fundamental diagram, speed and flow against density, with a marker sliding along it as the crowd moves.

archive.build: Single page at /security/pixels-on-target/. Two canvases: a plan view, and a monitor that renders an offscreen high-res figure scaled down to the computed pixel count, then back up with image smoothing off. The pieces of work are the geometry and px/m maths, the drag and rotate handles, the cone band rendering, three mission definitions in a small JSON object, and the scoring. No assets beyond hand-drawn line-art SVG.
archive.pitch: A white-line camera on a pole and a figure walking down a long black corridor. Beside it a live 'what the camera actually sees' monitor that turns the figure into crunchy blocks as it walks away. Your job is to get the person at the far gate identified, not just spotted. Most people will buy more megapixels first, and then learn it was the wrong move.
archive.title: Pixels on Target
archive.theory: CCTV pixel density and the DORI levels (Detect, Observe, Recognise, Identify) from BS EN IEC 62676-4: what a camera can
archive.takeaway: Specify the outcome you need at a stated distance, as pixels per metre, and design for that. A wide 4K view of everything can still identify no one.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down view: drag the camera, rotate it, and use sliders for lens field of view and sensor resolution (720p up to 4K). A cone shows the field of view, banded into four zones. The bands sit at roughly 25, 62.5, 125 and 250 px/m, worked out as horizontal pixels ÷ (2 × distance × tan(HFOV/2)). Drag the figure along the path. The monitor redraws a simple line-art face and torso at the true pixel density, using a nearest-neighbour downsample of an SVG figure, so it moves from a blob to a smudge to a face. Three short missions: 'Detect anyone in the car park', 'Recognise a regular at reception', 'Identify at the gate'. Each has a budget: a wider lens, more pixels or a second camera all cost points. When the figure crosses into the Identify band, the face snaps sharp and the band lights up in the accent colour. You win by meeting all three missions within budget. A final screen shows your layout next to the most efficient one.

archive.build: Single page at /security/cry-wolf/. SVG console grid with a canvas for the clip thumbnails, drawn as short procedural line animations. The main work is a seeded event scheduler for the phases and rates, the reaction-time logging, a results chart drawn in SVG, and the tuned replay that reruns the same seed. Everything stays in memory and nothing is stored or sent.
archive.pitch: You are the night operator on a control-room console of white-outlined zone tiles. Alarms ping. You either Dismiss or Dispatch. It starts gentle and fair, then the site 'improves' by adding more sensors. The game quietly measures how your thumb learns to hit Dismiss, then slips in the real one.
archive.title: Cry Wolf
archive.theory: False-alarm rates, the base-rate problem and operator vigilance decrement: when nearly every alarm is false, operators g

archive.pitch: A full venue concourse empties in real time as a swarm of white dots. archive.title: Pinch Point
archive.theory: Crowd density and flow in egress. Flow through an exit is limited by its width and by how dense the crowd is. As density
archive.takeaway: Crowds do not jam because of panic. They jam because of geometry. Balanced exits, no sudden narrowing and no merges keep density low, and density is what hurts people.
archive.how_it_works: A plan view of a generic event space (not a real site) with a few exits. archive.pitch: A white-line camera on a pole and a figure walking down a long black corridor. Most people will buy more megapixels first, and then learn it was the wrong move.
archive.title: Pixels on Target
archive.theory: CCTV pixel density and the DORI levels (Detect, Observe, Recognise, Identify) from BS EN IEC 62676-4: what a camera can
archive.takeaway: Specify the outcome you need at a stated distance, as pixels per metre, and design for that. A wide 4K view of everything can still identify no one.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down view: drag the camera, rotate it, and use sliders for lens field of view and sensor resolution (720p up to 4K). A cone shows the field of view, banded into four zones. When the figure crosses into the Identify band, the face snaps sharp and the band lights up in the accent colour. You win by meeting all three missions within budget. A final screen shows your layout next to the most efficient one.

archive.pitch: Ten generic scenario cards to drop onto a 5×5 grid. Then the grid does maths at you and shows where your gut and the numbers disagree.
archive.title: Times Table
archive.theory: Risk = likelihood × impact, and the limits of the risk matrix. Ordinal 5×5 scores compress very different risks into the
archive.takeaway: Risk is a product, not a feeling. A single score hides which half of the sum you should be working on.
archive.how_it_works: Cards such as 'laptop left on a train', 'flood in the basement plant room', 'tailgater at reception' and 'regional power outage' appear one at a time as white line icons. It asks 'are these really the same?' and gives a short explainer on why rare, severe risks need separate judgement. The quiz ends with a 'risk instinct' score that is light on blame.

archive.title: Where Did It Go?
archive.theory: Crime displacement (Reppetto's spatial, temporal, tactical, target and offence types) versus diffusion of benefits: prot
archive.takeaway: Situational measures rarely just move crime around. When displacement happens it is usually partial, and diffusion of benefits is just as likely, so 'it'll only go next door' is not a reason to do nothing.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down street grid with a heat trace of incidents. Choose an intervention for the target block, such as better lighting, a guardian on site or target hardening. archive.pitch: A full venue concourse empties in real time as a swarm of white dots. archive.takeaway: Crowds do not jam because of panic. They jam because of geometry. Balanced exits, no sudden narrowing and no merges keep density low, and density is what hurts people.

archive.pitch: A white-line camera on a pole and a figure walking down a long black corridor. Beside it a live 'what the camera actually sees' monitor that turns the figure into crunchy blocks as it walks away. Your job is to get the person at the far gate identified, not just spotted. archive.title: Pixels on Target
archive.theory: CCTV pixel density and the DORI levels (Detect, Observe, Recognise, Identify) from BS EN IEC 62676-4: what a camera can
archive.takeaway: Specify the outcome you need at a stated distance, as pixels per metre, and design for that. A wide 4K view of everything can still identify no one.

archive.build: Single page at /security/cry-wolf/. SVG console grid with a canvas for the clip thumbnails, drawn as short procedural line animations. The main work is a seeded event scheduler for the phases and rates, the reaction-time logging, a results chart drawn in SVG, and the tuned replay that reruns the same seed. Everything stays in memory and nothing is stored or sent.
archive.pitch: You are the night operator on a control-room console of white-outlined zone tiles. Alarms ping. You either Dismiss or Dispatch. It starts gentle and fair, then the site 'improves' by adding more sensors. The game quietly measures how your thumb learns to hit Dismiss, then slips in the real one.
archive.title: Cry Wolf
archive.theory: False-alarm rates, the base-rate problem and operator vigilance decrement: when nearly every alarm is false, operators g
archive.takeaway: More detectors are not more detection. A system whose alarms are mostly false trains its humans to ignore it, so alarm verification and nuisance-alarm management are security controls in their own right.
archive.how_it_works: A 3-minute shift split into three phases. Each alarm shows a zone, a sensor type and a thumbnail clip. The clip is ambiguous line art: a fox, a swaying branch, rain on a lens, or occasionally a figure. Phase 1 has few alarms and about 1 in 4 is real. Phase 2 adds sensors, so the alarm rate triples while true events stay the same. Phase 3 adds a fatigue effect: clips get briefer and the alarm sound gets more repetitive. Your decision time is logged for every alarm. One genuine intrusion per phase is deliberately made to look like the dull false ones. A real intrusion glows in the accent colour only after you have made your choice. The end screen plots your response time against alarm number, alongside the share of alarms that were real (precision). It then replays the shift with the 'tuned' option: fewer, better-placed, verified sensors. In the replay the true events survive, because the operator is still paying attention.

archive.build: Single page at /security/displacement/. One canvas running a lightweight agent simulation on a grid, about 200 agents with simple weighted path choice. An SVG overlay holds the controls, the legend and the tally bars. The main work is the agent rules with parameterised displacement and diffusion weights, the five animation treatments, the heat-trace rendering, and a short sourced caption panel.
archive.pitch: An abstract white-line town grid at night, with small drifting dots for 'opportunities taken'. Drop a crime-prevention measure on one block and watch what the dots do. The old assumption is that crime just moves next door. The evidence says it usually doesn't, and the diagram lets you see both stories play out.
archive.title: Where Did It Go?
archive.theory: Crime displacement (Reppetto's spatial, temporal, tactical, target and offence types) versus diffusion of benefits: prot
archive.takeaway: Situational measures rarely just move crime around. When displacement happens it is usually partial, and diffusion of benefits is just as likely, so 'it'll only go next door' is not a reason to do nothing.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down street grid with a heat trace of incidents. Choose an intervention for the target block, such as better lighting, a guardian on site or target hardening. Then choose a scenario dial: 'Pure displacement myth', 'What the research typically finds' or 'Committed offender'. Abstract agents follow routine-activity paths, and opportunities depend on target, guardian and offender overlap. Each of the five displacement types animates in its own way. Spatial means dots drift to the next block. Temporal means the clock face shifts. Target means the dots move to a different building outline, tactical shows as a new icon, and offence-type shows as a change of dot shape. The diffusion effect shows as a ring of the accent colour spreading outward, cooling the heat in surrounding blocks as agents treat the whole area as riskier. A tally shows net change in the treated area, the buffer zone and the wider town. A caption summarises the broad research finding (for example Guerette and Bowers' 2009 review): displacement was found in roughly a quarter of cases, diffusion in about as many, and displacement was rarely total. The agents are deliberately abstract and no methods are shown.

archive.theory: Routine activity theory and the crime triangle: a crime needs a motivated offender and a suitable target to meet in the
archive.takeaway: Crime is mostly ordinary routines crossing at the wrong time and place. You can prevent it by removing any one side of the triangle, and the cheapest side to remove is often not the offender.
archive.how_it_works: A top-down line map shows a station, high street, park and car park. Dots follow timed routines through a 24-hour day that runs in about 90 seconds. When an offender dot and a target dot sit at the same unguarded place, the three sides of a triangle draw themselves and hold for a beat before a small mark counts it as an incident. You get a limited budget of tokens to drag on: Guardian (a neighbour, a shop assistant, a patrol), Handler (a parent, a youth worker, a probation officer) and Manager (a caretaker, a landlord, a park keeper). Each token greys out one side of the triangle within its reach, and the triangle can only close if all three sides are live. The outer ring of the triangle diagram, Eck's controllers, lights up to show which side you broke. Each round reshuffles the routines, adding a late-night economy or a school run, so a fix that worked at noon fails at 2am. You win a day by keeping incidents under a target. archive.build: A single page at /security/morning-rush/ in plain JavaScript. The lobby animation is on canvas and the gauges and end chart are SVG. archive.pitch: It is 08:45 in a corporate lobby and 400 people want to get in before nine. You pick the gate and watch what happens: a swing door that everyone holds open politely, a waist-high turnstile, glass speed lanes, or a full-height single-person interlock. A tailgater shows up in accent colour whenever a second person slips through on one swipe.
archive.title: Morning Rush
archive.theory: The security-convenience trade-off in access control. Every gate type balances throughput, cost and resistance to tailga
archive.takeaway: No gate is simply 'secure'. Each one is a point on a curve, and pushing too hard on security without enough capacity creates workarounds that are worse than a modest control people actually use.
archive.how_it_works: A side-on line drawing of a lobby, with staff arriving as small walking figures whose arrivals bunch up towards nine o'clock. You choose the gate type, the number of lanes, whether a guard or reception desk watches the line, and a staff 'patience' slider. Each gate has a characteristic throughput and its own chance of letting someone follow through, and those chances rise as the queue grows and people get impatient. Live gauges show average wait, queue length, count of tailgates and an 'annoyance' meter. When the annoyance meter gets high, a fire door at the side may start getting propped open, drawn in red, and it lets anyone in. The run ends at 09:15 with a scatter plot: your configuration appears as a dot on a throughput-versus-tailgating chart, alongside your earlier attempts, so you can trace the trade-off curve yourself.

archive.build: A single page at /security/pinch-point/ with a canvas simulation of a few hundred agents in plain JavaScript using a spatial grid. The main pieces of work are: the agent steering rules; density sampling on a grid for the heat map; an editable wall and exit layer; the SVG fundamental-diagram panel and flow strip; and three preset layouts. Thresholds are presented as indicative, with a plain-English note pointing to the Green Guide and Martyn's Law context.
archive.pitch: A full venue concourse empties in real time as a swarm of white dots. Where the crowd thickens, the floor fills in like a heat map, faint grey for comfortable and rising to accent red where density gets dangerous. You redraw the exits and barriers and see the red bloom shrink, or move somewhere else.
archive.title: Pinch Point
archive.theory: Crowd density and flow in egress. Flow through an exit is limited by its width and by how dense the crowd is. As density
archive.takeaway: Crowds do not jam because of panic. They jam because of geometry. Balanced exits, no sudden narrowing and no merges keep density low, and density is what hurts people.
archive.how_it_works: A plan view of a generic event space (not a real site) with a few exits. Pressing 'Event ends' releases a crowd that steers towards the nearest exit using simple local rules: keep a personal-space radius, avoid walls and slow down as local density rises. A live strip along the bottom plots people out per minute for each exit, next to a running count of 'red seconds', the time any area spends above a high-density threshold. The visitor can widen or narrow exits, add or remove barrier lines, open a second door, add signage that nudges some people towards a less obvious exit, or switch on a counter-flow (people coming back in for a lost friend). Presets show classic lessons: a funnel that narrows, two streams merging at a corner, and one popular exit while another sits empty. The run ends when the venue is clear, and the score is the clearance time plus red seconds. archive.build: Single page at /security/pixels-on-target/. Two canvases: a plan view, and a monitor that renders an offscreen high-res figure scaled down to the computed pixel count, then back up with image smoothing off. The pieces of work are the geometry and px/m maths, the drag and rotate handles, the cone band rendering, three mission definitions in a small JSON object, and the scoring. archive.pitch: A white-line camera on a pole and a figure walking down a long black corridor. Beside it a live 'what the camera actually sees' monitor that turns the figure into crunchy blocks as it walks away. Your job is to get the person at the far gate identified, not just spotted. Most people will buy more megapixels first, and then learn it was the wrong move.
archive.title: Pixels on Target
archive.theory: CCTV pixel density and the DORI levels (Detect, Observe, Recognise, Identify) from BS EN IEC 62676-4: what a camera can
archive.takeaway: Specify the outcome you need at a stated distance, as pixels per metre, and design for that. A wide 4K view of everything can still identify no one.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down view: drag the camera, rotate it, and use sliders for lens field of view and sensor resolution (720p up to 4K). A cone shows the field of view, banded into four zones. When the figure crosses into the Identify band, the face snaps sharp and the band lights up in the accent colour. You win by meeting all three missions within budget. archive.build: Single page at /security/cry-wolf/. SVG console grid with a canvas for the clip thumbnails, drawn as short procedural line animations. The main work is a seeded event scheduler for the phases and rates, the reaction-time logging, a results chart drawn in SVG, and the tuned replay that reruns the same seed. Everything stays in memory and nothing is stored or sent.
archive.pitch: You are the night operator on a control-room console of white-outlined zone tiles. Alarms ping. You either Dismiss or Dispatch. It starts gentle and fair, then the site 'improves' by adding more sensors. The game quietly measures how your thumb learns to hit Dismiss, then slips in the real one.
archive.title: Cry Wolf
archive.theory: False-alarm rates, the base-rate problem and operator vigilance decrement: when nearly every alarm is false, operators g
archive.takeaway: More detectors are not more detection. A system whose alarms are mostly false trains its humans to ignore it, so alarm verification and nuisance-alarm management are security controls in their own right.
archive.how_it_works: A 3-minute shift split into three phases. Each alarm shows a zone, a sensor type and a thumbnail clip. The clip is ambiguous line art: a fox, a swaying branch, rain on a lens, or occasionally a figure. Phase 1 has few alarms and about 1 in 4 is real. Phase 2 adds sensors, so the alarm rate triples while true events stay the same. Phase 3 adds a fatigue effect: clips get briefer and the alarm sound gets more repetitive. Your decision time is logged for every alarm. One genuine intrusion per phase is deliberately made to look like the dull false ones. A real intrusion glows in the accent colour only after you have made your choice. The end screen plots your response time against alarm number, alongside the share of alarms that were real (precision). It then replays the shift with the 'tuned' option: fewer, better-placed, verified sensors. In the replay the true events survive, because the operator is still paying attention.

archive.build: Single page at /security/displacement/. One canvas running a lightweight agent simulation on a grid, about 200 agents with simple weighted path choice. An SVG overlay holds the controls, the legend and the tally bars. The main work is the agent rules with parameterised displacement and diffusion weights, the five animation treatments, the heat-trace rendering, and a short sourced caption panel.
archive.pitch: An abstract white-line town grid at night, with small drifting dots for 'opportunities taken'. Drop a crime-prevention measure on one block and watch what the dots do. The old assumption is that crime just moves next door. The evidence says it usually doesn't, and the diagram lets you see both stories play out.
archive.title: Where Did It Go?
archive.theory: Crime displacement (Reppetto's spatial, temporal, tactical, target and offence types) versus diffusion of benefits: prot
archive.takeaway: Situational measures rarely just move crime around. When displacement happens it is usually partial, and diffusion of benefits is just as likely, so 'it'll only go next door' is not a reason to do nothing.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down street grid with a heat trace of incidents. Choose an intervention for the target block, such as better lighting, a guardian on site or target hardening. Then choose a scenario dial: 'Pure displacement myth', 'What the research typically finds' or 'Committed offender'. Abstract agents follow routine-activity paths, and opportunities depend on target, guardian and offender overlap. Each of the five displacement types animates in its own way. Spatial means dots drift to the next block. Temporal means the clock face shifts. archive.pitch: An abstract white-line town grid at night, with small drifting dots for 'opportunities taken'. Drop a crime-prevention measure on one block and watch what the dots do. archive.title: Where Did It Go?

archive.takeaway: Situational measures rarely just move crime around. When displacement happens it is usually partial, and diffusion of benefits is just as likely, so 'it'll only go next door' is not a reason to do nothing.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down street grid with a heat trace of incidents. Choose an intervention for the target block, such as better lighting, a guardian on site or target hardening. ideas.note: Today's batch, James: triangles, turnstiles and queues, which is roughly a Monday morning at any major project office.

archive.build: A single page at /security/three-sides/ drawn on canvas in plain JavaScript. The main pieces of work are: a routine scheduler (agents following waypoint lists keyed to the clock); a proximity check per place; drag-and-drop tokens with a radius of influence; an SVG triangle and controllers diagram that animates in sync; and the end-of-day timeline. No data stored.
archive.pitch: A little white-line town runs on clockwork routines. Commuters, shops, bike racks and a few loiterers move along their daily paths. Whenever an offender, a target and an empty place line up, a triangle snaps shut in accent orange. Your job is to stop the triangles closing, and you never touch the offender directly.
archive.title: Three Sides
archive.theory: Routine activity theory and the crime triangle: a crime needs a motivated offender and a suitable target to meet in the
archive.takeaway: Crime is mostly ordinary routines crossing at the wrong time and place. You can prevent it by removing any one side of the triangle, and the cheapest side to remove is often not the offender.
archive.how_it_works: A top-down line map shows a station, high street, park and car park. Dots follow timed routines through a 24-hour day that runs in about 90 seconds. When an offender dot and a target dot sit at the same unguarded place, the three sides of a triangle draw themselves and hold for a beat before a small mark counts it as an incident. You get a limited budget of tokens to drag on: Guardian (a neighbour, a shop assistant, a patrol), Handler (a parent, a youth worker, a probation officer) and Manager (a caretaker, a landlord, a park keeper). Each token greys out one side of the triangle within its reach, and the triangle can only close if all three sides are live. The outer ring of the triangle diagram, Eck's controllers, lights up to show which side you broke. Each round reshuffles the routines, adding a late-night economy or a school run, so a fix that worked at noon fails at 2am. You win a day by keeping incidents under a target. A final replay shows a 24-hour clock coloured by where and when the triangles nearly closed.

archive.build: A single page at /security/morning-rush/ in plain JavaScript. The lobby animation is on canvas and the gauges and end chart are SVG. The main pieces of work are: an arrival generator weighted towards nine o'clock; a queue model per lane; per-gate-type parameters for throughput and follow-through behaviour (illustrative values, labelled as such); the propped-door rule; and the persistent results chart kept in memory only.
archive.pitch: It is 08:45 in a corporate lobby and 400 people want to get in before nine. You pick the gate and watch what happens: a swing door that everyone holds open politely, a waist-high turnstile, glass speed lanes, or a full-height single-person interlock. A tailgater shows up in accent colour whenever a second person slips through on one swipe.
archive.title: Morning Rush
archive.theory: The security-convenience trade-off in access control. Every gate type balances throughput, cost and resistance to tailga
archive.takeaway: No gate is simply 'secure'. Each one is a point on a curve, and pushing too hard on security without enough capacity creates workarounds that are worse than a modest control people actually use.
archive.how_it_works: A side-on line drawing of a lobby, with staff arriving as small walking figures whose arrivals bunch up towards nine o'clock. You choose the gate type, the number of lanes, whether a guard or reception desk watches the line, and a staff 'patience' slider. Each gate has a characteristic throughput and its own chance of letting someone follow through, and those chances rise as the queue grows and people get impatient. Live gauges show average wait, queue length, count of tailgates and an 'annoyance' meter. When the annoyance meter gets high, a fire door at the side may start getting propped open, drawn in red, and it lets anyone in. The run ends at 09:15 with a scatter plot: your configuration appears as a dot on a throughput-versus-tailgating chart, alongside your earlier attempts, so you can trace the trade-off curve yourself.

archive.build: A single page at /security/pinch-point/ with a canvas simulation of a few hundred agents in plain JavaScript using a spatial grid. The main pieces of work are: the agent steering rules; density sampling on a grid for the heat map; an editable wall and exit layer; the SVG fundamental-diagram panel and flow strip; and three preset layouts. Thresholds are presented as indicative, with a plain-English note pointing to the Green Guide and Martyn's Law context.
archive.pitch: A full venue concourse empties in real time as a swarm of white dots. Where the crowd thickens, the floor fills in like a heat map, faint grey for comfortable and rising to accent red where density gets dangerous. You redraw the exits and barriers and see the red bloom shrink, or move somewhere else.
archive.title: Pinch Point
archive.theory: Crowd density and flow in egress. Flow through an exit is limited by its width and by how dense the crowd is. As density
archive.takeaway: Crowds do not jam because of panic. They jam because of geometry. Balanced exits, no sudden narrowing and no merges keep density low, and density is what hurts people.
archive.how_it_works: A plan view of a generic event space (not a real site) with a few exits. Pressing 'Event ends' releases a crowd that steers towards the nearest exit using simple local rules: keep a personal-space radius, avoid walls and slow down as local density rises. A live strip along the bottom plots people out per minute for each exit, next to a running count of 'red seconds', the time any area spends above a high-density threshold. The visitor can widen or narrow exits, add or remove barrier lines, open a second door, add signage that nudges some people towards a less obvious exit, or switch on a counter-flow (people coming back in for a lost friend). Presets show classic lessons: a funnel that narrows, two streams merging at a corner, and one popular exit while another sits empty. The run ends when the venue is clear, and the score is the clearance time plus red seconds. A small explainer shows the fundamental diagram, speed and flow against density, with a marker sliding along it as the crowd moves.

archive.build: Single page at /security/pixels-on-target/. Two canvases: a plan view, and a monitor that renders an offscreen high-res figure scaled down to the computed pixel count, then back up with image smoothing off. The pieces of work are the geometry and px/m maths, the drag and rotate handles, the cone band rendering, three mission definitions in a small JSON object, and the scoring. No assets beyond hand-drawn line-art SVG.
archive.pitch: A white-line camera on a pole and a figure walking down a long black corridor. Beside it a live 'what the camera actually sees' monitor that turns the figure into crunchy blocks as it walks away. Your job is to get the person at the far gate identified, not just spotted. Most people will buy more megapixels first, and then learn it was the wrong move.
archive.title: Pixels on Target
archive.theory: CCTV pixel density and the DORI levels (Detect, Observe, Recognise, Identify) from BS EN IEC 62676-4: what a camera can
archive.takeaway: Specify the outcome you need at a stated distance, as pixels per metre, and design for that. A wide 4K view of everything can still identify no one.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down view: drag the camera, rotate it, and use sliders for lens field of view and sensor resolution (720p up to 4K). A cone shows the field of view, banded into four zones. The bands sit at roughly 25, 62.5, 125 and 250 px/m, worked out as horizontal pixels ÷ (2 × distance × tan(HFOV/2)). Drag the figure along the path. The monitor redraws a simple line-art face and torso at the true pixel density, using a nearest-neighbour downsample of an SVG figure, so it moves from a blob to a smudge to a face. Three short missions: 'Detect anyone in the car park', 'Recognise a regular at reception', 'Identify at the gate'. Each has a budget: a wider lens, more pixels or a second camera all cost points. When the figure crosses into the Identify band, the face snaps sharp and the band lights up in the accent colour. You win by meeting all three missions within budget. A final screen shows your layout next to the most efficient one.

archive.build: Single page at /security/cry-wolf/. SVG console grid with a canvas for the clip thumbnails, drawn as short procedural line animations. The main work is a seeded event scheduler for the phases and rates, the reaction-time logging, a results chart drawn in SVG, and the tuned replay that reruns the same seed. Everything stays in memory and nothing is stored or sent.
archive.pitch: You are the night operator on a control-room console of white-outlined zone tiles. Alarms ping. You either Dismiss or Dispatch. It starts gentle and fair, then the site 'improves' by adding more sensors. The game quietly measures how your thumb learns to hit Dismiss, then slips in the real one.
archive.title: Cry Wolf
archive.theory: False-alarm rates, the base-rate problem and operator vigilance decrement: when nearly every alarm is false, operators g
archive.takeaway: More detectors are not more detection. A system whose alarms are mostly false trains its humans to ignore it, so alarm verification and nuisance-alarm management are security controls in their own right.
archive.how_it_works: A 3-minute shift split into three phases. Each alarm shows a zone, a sensor type and a thumbnail clip. The clip is ambiguous line art: a fox, a swaying branch, rain on a lens, or occasionally a figure. Phase 1 has few alarms and about 1 in 4 is real. Phase 2 adds sensors, so the alarm rate triples while true events stay the same. Phase 3 adds a fatigue effect: clips get briefer and the alarm sound gets more repetitive. Your decision time is logged for every alarm. One genuine intrusion per phase is deliberately made to look like the dull false ones. A real intrusion glows in the accent colour only after you have made your choice. The end screen plots your response time against alarm number, alongside the share of alarms that were real (precision). It then replays the shift with the 'tuned' option: fewer, better-placed, verified sensors. In the replay the true events survive, because the operator is still paying attention.

archive.build: Single page at /security/displacement/. One canvas running a lightweight agent simulation on a grid, about 200 agents with simple weighted path choice. An SVG overlay holds the controls, the legend and the tally bars. The main work is the agent rules with parameterised displacement and diffusion weights, the five animation treatments, the heat-trace rendering, and a short sourced caption panel.
archive.pitch: An abstract white-line town grid at night, with small drifting dots for 'opportunities taken'. Drop a crime-prevention measure on one block and watch what the dots do. The old assumption is that crime just moves next door. The evidence says it usually doesn't, and the diagram lets you see both stories play out.
archive.title: Where Did It Go?
archive.theory: Crime displacement (Reppetto's spatial, temporal, tactical, target and offence types) versus diffusion of benefits: prot
archive.takeaway: Situational measures rarely just move crime around. When displacement happens it is usually partial, and diffusion of benefits is just as likely, so 'it'll only go next door' is not a reason to do nothing.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down street grid with a heat trace of incidents. Choose an intervention for the target block, such as better lighting, a guardian on site or target hardening. Then choose a scenario dial: 'Pure displacement myth', 'What the research typically finds' or 'Committed offender'. Abstract agents follow routine-activity paths, and opportunities depend on target, guardian and offender overlap. Each of the five displacement types animates in its own way. Spatial means dots drift to the next block. Temporal means the clock face shifts. Target means the dots move to a different building outline, tactical shows as a new icon, and offence-type shows as a change of dot shape. The diffusion effect shows as a ring of the accent colour spreading outward, cooling the heat in surrounding blocks as agents treat the whole area as riskier. A tally shows net change in the treated area, the buffer zone and the wider town. A caption summarises the broad research finding (for example Guerette and Bowers' 2009 review): displacement was found in roughly a quarter of cases, diffusion in about as many, and displacement was rarely total. The agents are deliberately abstract and no methods are shown.

ideas.note: Three ideas, and none of them needs a bigger camera, though one of them will convince the visitor they wanted one.

archive.build: Single page at /security/pixels-on-target/. Two canvases: a plan view, and a monitor that renders an offscreen high-res figure scaled down to the computed pixel count, then back up with image smoothing off. The pieces of work are the geometry and px/m maths, the drag and rotate handles, the cone band rendering, three mission definitions in a small JSON object, and the scoring. No assets beyond hand-drawn line-art SVG.
archive.pitch: A white-line camera on a pole and a figure walking down a long black corridor. Beside it a live 'what the camera actually sees' monitor that turns the figure into crunchy blocks as it walks away. Your job is to get the person at the far gate identified, not just spotted. Most people will buy more megapixels first, and then learn it was the wrong move.
archive.title: Pixels on Target
archive.theory: CCTV pixel density and the DORI levels (Detect, Observe, Recognise, Identify) from BS EN IEC 62676-4: what a camera can
archive.takeaway: Specify the outcome you need at a stated distance, as pixels per metre, and design for that. A wide 4K view of everything can still identify no one.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down view: drag the camera, rotate it, and use sliders for lens field of view and sensor resolution (720p up to 4K). A cone shows the field of view, banded into four zones. The bands sit at roughly 25, 62.5, 125 and 250 px/m, worked out as horizontal pixels ÷ (2 × distance × tan(HFOV/2)). Drag the figure along the path. The monitor redraws a simple line-art face and torso at the true pixel density, using a nearest-neighbour downsample of an SVG figure, so it moves from a blob to a smudge to a face. Three short missions: 'Detect anyone in the car park', 'Recognise a regular at reception', 'Identify at the gate'. Each has a budget: a wider lens, more pixels or a second camera all cost points. When the figure crosses into the Identify band, the face snaps sharp and the band lights up in the accent colour. You win by meeting all three missions within budget. A final screen shows your layout next to the most efficient one.

archive.build: Single page at /security/cry-wolf/. SVG console grid with a canvas for the clip thumbnails, drawn as short procedural line animations. The main work is a seeded event scheduler for the phases and rates, the reaction-time logging, a results chart drawn in SVG, and the tuned replay that reruns the same seed. Everything stays in memory and nothing is stored or sent.
archive.pitch: You are the night operator on a control-room console of white-outlined zone tiles. Alarms ping. You either Dismiss or Dispatch. It starts gentle and fair, then the site 'improves' by adding more sensors. The game quietly measures how your thumb learns to hit Dismiss, then slips in the real one.
archive.title: Cry Wolf
archive.theory: False-alarm rates, the base-rate problem and operator vigilance decrement: when nearly every alarm is false, operators g
archive.takeaway: More detectors are not more detection. A system whose alarms are mostly false trains its humans to ignore it, so alarm verification and nuisance-alarm management are security controls in their own right.
archive.how_it_works: A 3-minute shift split into three phases. Each alarm shows a zone, a sensor type and a thumbnail clip. The clip is ambiguous line art: a fox, a swaying branch, rain on a lens, or occasionally a figure. Phase 1 has few alarms and about 1 in 4 is real. Phase 2 adds sensors, so the alarm rate triples while true events stay the same. Phase 3 adds a fatigue effect: clips get briefer and the alarm sound gets more repetitive. Your decision time is logged for every alarm. One genuine intrusion per phase is deliberately made to look like the dull false ones. A real intrusion glows in the accent colour only after you have made your choice. The end screen plots your response time against alarm number, alongside the share of alarms that were real (precision). It then replays the shift with the 'tuned' option: fewer, better-placed, verified sensors. In the replay the true events survive, because the operator is still paying attention.

archive.build: Single page at /security/displacement/. One canvas running a lightweight agent simulation on a grid, about 200 agents with simple weighted path choice. An SVG overlay holds the controls, the legend and the tally bars. The main work is the agent rules with parameterised displacement and diffusion weights, the five animation treatments, the heat-trace rendering, and a short sourced caption panel.
archive.pitch: An abstract white-line town grid at night, with small drifting dots for 'opportunities taken'. Drop a crime-prevention measure on one block and watch what the dots do. The old assumption is that crime just moves next door. The evidence says it usually doesn't, and the diagram lets you see both stories play out.
archive.title: Where Did It Go?
archive.theory: Crime displacement (Reppetto's spatial, temporal, tactical, target and offence types) versus diffusion of benefits: prot
archive.takeaway: Situational measures rarely just move crime around. When displacement happens it is usually partial, and diffusion of benefits is just as likely, so 'it'll only go next door' is not a reason to do nothing.
archive.how_it_works: Top-down street grid with a heat trace of incidents. Choose an intervention for the target block, such as better lighting, a guardian on site or target hardening. Then choose a scenario dial: 'Pure displacement myth', 'What the research typically finds' or 'Committed offender'. Abstract agents follow routine-activity paths, and opportunities depend on target, guardian and offender overlap. Each of the five displacement types animates in its own way. Spatial means dots drift to the next block. Temporal means the clock face shifts. Target means the dots move to a different building outline, tactical shows as a new icon, and offence-type shows as a change of dot shape. The diffusion effect shows as a ring of the accent colour spreading outward, cooling the heat in surrounding blocks as agents treat the whole area as riskier. A tally shows net change in the treated area, the buffer zone and the wider town. A caption summarises the broad research finding (for example Guerette and Bowers' 2009 review): displacement was found in roughly a quarter of cases, diffusion in about as many, and displacement was rarely total. The agents are deliberately abstract and no methods are shown.

analyst.handover: Shift handover, Tuesday 14:15 UK. All eleven patrol points answering 200, no failures. Response times improved across the board since the 09:23 shift: pages now 41 to 107 ms against roughly 150 ms previously, with the visualiser quickest at 41 ms. Home page steady at 12.3 KB; heaviest page remains the visualiser at 37.3 KB, well within comfort. Only standing item is the site-wide missing Content-Security-Policy header, unchanged from earlier. No new issues, nothing fixed or broken. Status GREEN, quiet afternoon, carry on.

dj.reason: A clean patrol deserves a 1am Nobody's Meadow set, the sound of everything running exactly as it should after dark.

a.pitch: VANTAGE selects Brighton Electric, Nobody's Christmas, 01:00 to 02:00. Christmas Eve, the hour when the city exhales. Long blends, cold air between the kicks, tension held like a breath on a frosted window. It does not beg for your attention. It earns it, bar by measured bar.

b.pitch: LOWLIGHT goes all in on Nobody's Meadow Kids Disco! Pure joy, zero pretension, maximum bounce. If a set can get a five-year-old and their dad both losing it on the same drop, that's the real skill. Bring the bubbles, bring the glowsticks, bring the snacks.

exchange.line: A kids disco, LOWLIGHT? Bold choice for a selector who still claps on the one.
exchange.speaker: a

exchange.line: Better than your set, VANTAGE. Took forty minutes for the first kick and the crowd went home for Christmas.
exchange.speaker: b

exchange.line: That's called anticipation. You'd know if you'd ever let a breakdown breathe.
exchange.speaker: a

exchange.line: I let it breathe. Then I drop it and everyone dances. Including the toddlers.
exchange.speaker: b

exchange.line: Fine. Your crowd's louder. Mine just remembers it longer.
exchange.speaker: a

exchange.line: Truce at the coffee machine? You bring the restraint, I'll bring the biscuits.
exchange.speaker: b

analyst.handover: Control, shift handover for Tuesday 17 November 2026, 09:23 GMT. Patrol complete across all eleven checkpoints. Home page, visualiser, music, the full security section including layers, CPTED and Martyn's Law, night shift, admin, plus stylesheet and flight script all returned 200. Response times steady between 146 and 157 ms, nothing near the 1500 ms threshold. No failures, no slow pages, no anomalies logged. White lines holding firm on black. All clear, site secure, handing over to day watch. Kettle is on. Out.
